findings_summary: States that one molecule of apoB-100 encircles each VLDL, LDL and Lp(a) particle (text: 'One molecule of apo B 100 encircles VLDL, LDL, and Lp(a) particles'), that each LDL particle derives from a VLDL particle, and that apoB-100 is 550 kDa. On that basis plasma apoB concentration is a count of atherogenic particles, while cholesterol per particle varies.

limitations.text: Narrative review by authors who advocate ApoB; claims are the authors' statements, not new data.
The 550 kDa figure is cited by the review, not measured in it; converting mg/dL to particle concentration depends on this value and on the assay's calibration.

applicability_constraints: Physiological premises, not a clinical outcome study.
Assumes fasting conditions in which apoB-48 particles are negligible.

discrepancies.description: The review gives apoB-100 as 4136 amino acids; the commonly cited mature apoB-100 length is 4536. Likely a typographical error in the review.
locations: apoB Particles and apoB Particle Number, first paragraph
discrepancies.handling: Not relied on; only the 550 kDa value is used, and the conversion it supports is labelled as dependent on that value.

interpretation: If each atherogenic particle carries one apoB-100, apoB in mg/dL can be expressed as a particle concentration (about 18.2 nmol/L per mg/dL at 550 kDa). LDL particles are a subset of apoB-containing particles, so an accurate LDL particle number should not exceed that total. More small LDL particles can raise LDL particle number relative to LDL cholesterol, but cannot by themselves make LDL particle number exceed the apoB particle count.
